units.title: Least squares: residuals, normal equations and stable solvers
outcomes: Derive the normal equations from the squared-error objective and state when the solution is unique.
Implement least squares three ways (normal equations, SVD least squares, minibatch gradient descent) with a gradient check, and match them on well-conditioned data.
Explain why squared loss punishes large residuals quadratically and when that sensitivity becomes a liability.
units.why: Least squares is the baseline every later model is compared against. Its two failure modes, singular designs and outlier sensitivity, recur in every fitting method after it.

next.note: Repair the singular and badly scaled designs met here with standardization and penalties.
Read residuals and leverage on the fits built here.

study.title: Normal equation and batch gradient descent
study.locator: Book Chapter 4: The Normal Equation (printed pp. 138-141) and Batch Gradient Descent (pp. 145-148). Notebook 04 cells: The Normal Equation section (theta_best with the explicit inverse, then the np.linalg.lstsq and pseudoinverse cross-checks) and Gradient Descent (the batch loop: gradient 2/m X_b'(X_b theta - y), eta 0.1, 1000 epochs from a random start)

focus: D2L scales its per-example loss by 1/2 while HoML differentiates the plain mean of squares with a 2/m gradient. The minimizer is identical but the largest stable learning rate differs by that constant.

X'Xw = X'y has a unique solution only when X has full column rank. With duplicate or nearly collinear columns the fitted values stay well determined but the coefficients do not: in the 1e-4 demo below both solvers return slopes near 229 and -228, and only their sum, 1.012, is pinned by the data.
The course notebooks show inv(X'X)@X'y to teach the formula; sklearn never forms that inverse and solves through the SVD instead.
units.reproduce: From ||y - Xw||^2, derive X'Xw = X'y on paper. Then build the near-collinear demo in NumPy: default_rng(1), n = 200, x1 standard normal, x2 = x1 + 1e-4 times standard normal noise, an intercept column, y = 3 + 2 x1 - x2 + 0.1 noise, drawn in that order. Show cond(X) = 2.08e4 and cond(X'X) = 4.34e8, its square. The explicit inverse and lstsq agree to about 1e-5, but both return about [3.002, 229.2, -228.2], not [3, 2, -1]. Then rebuild with default_rng(0), n = 60, x2 = x1 + 1e-8 noise and y = 3 + 2 x1 + 0.5 noise: cond(X) = 1.8e8 and cond(X'X) = 3.25e15, and the explicit inverse stops at residual norm 3.8314 while lstsq reaches the minimum, 3.7978.
traps: Shipping inv(X'X)@X'y as the solver. Forming X'X squares the condition number, so a design with cond(X) near 1e8 makes X'X numerically singular near 1/eps in float64 while lstsq still minimizes the residual.

Hand-rolling a bias column while the differential test keeps fit_intercept=True. sklearn centers the columns, so your ones column becomes all zeros: it gets coefficient 0 and intercept_ takes the offset. Predictions agree but a coefficient-by-coefficient comparison fails. Drop the column or pass fit_intercept=False.

Reading the second Deep-ML 15 test as the exact solution. It expects [2.9699, 2.0078], the gradient-descent iterate after 1000 steps at lr 0.05; the exact minimizer is [3, 2]. Zero initialization and the exact update decide it.

selfTest.q: D2L multiplies its loss by 1/2 and HoML does not. Why is the minimizer unchanged but the stable learning rate different?
selfTest.a: The constant scales the loss and every gradient without moving the stationary point, so the optimum is identical. A fixed step size moves half as far per step under the 1/2 convention, so its stability limit on eta is twice as large.

selfTest.q: Two columns of X are identical. What happens to X'X, the coefficients and the predictions?
selfTest.a: X'X is singular so the coefficients are not unique. The fitted values Xw stay unique as the projection onto the column space, and SVD-based solvers return the minimum-norm coefficient vector.

selfTest.q: cond(X) is 2.08e4. What is cond(X'X), and at what point does the explicit inverse break down?
selfTest.a: About 4.34e8, the square of cond(X). The explicit inverse loses all precision once cond(X'X) approaches 1/eps, about 4.5e15 in float64, which needs only cond(X) near 7e7. At 1.8e8 it no longer reaches the least-squares minimum.

selfTest.q: One label is corrupted upward by 100. Why does the squared-loss fit move far, and which single change to the loss limits the damage?
selfTest.a: The quadratic penalty lets that one residual dominate the objective. An absolute-error loss grows only linearly with it, so the fit moves far less.

units.title: Conditioning, basis expansions, ridge, lasso and elastic net
outcomes: Derive the ridge closed form and predict how standardization changes the penalized solution.

Measure coefficient paths and validation error across the penalty strength on fixed splits and select it from evidence.
units.why: An unpenalized fit trusts every column equally, so one rescaled feature or one duplicated signal can swing the coefficients wildly. Bases and penalties decide what the model may express before more data can save it.

study.title: Polynomial regression and regularized linear models
study.locator: Book Chapter 4: Polynomial Regression (printed pp. 153-154) and Regularized Linear Models (pp. 159-167). Notebook 04 cells: Polynomial Regression, Ridge Regression, Lasso Regression, Elastic Net and Early Stopping sections, including the scale-and-regularization warning in the chapter Q and A

focus: Ridge adds alpha ||w||^2 to the raw RSS, while Lasso and ElasticNet add their alpha penalty to RSS/(2n), so alpha = 1 means very different strengths. Compare paths or CV errors, never raw alphas.

Penalties tax raw coefficient size. A feature with small numeric values, such as kilometers instead of meters, needs a larger weight for the same effect, so it pays more penalty and is shrunk harder. Standardize before penalizing and leave the intercept free.

Lasso lands on corners: the sklearn guide says it is likely to pick one of several correlated features at random, while elastic net is likely to keep both. D2L's d = 200, n = 20 demo shows weight decay rescuing a fit with more features than samples.
units.reproduce: Derive w = (X'X + alpha I)^{-1} X'y for centered data. Build the correlated demo: default_rng(2), n = 100, x1 and x2 standard normal, x3 = x1 + 0.1 noise, y = 2 x1 - 3 x2 + standard normal noise, drawn in that order. Show Ridge(alpha=1.0) matches the centered closed form to 1e-14 at [1.33909931, -3.06183881, 0.64520852]. Then show Lasso returns all zeros once alpha reaches max|Xc'yc|/n = 2.74, the x2 entry; just below it only x2 enters (-0.146 at alpha = 2.6). Ridge at any finite alpha keeps every coefficient nonzero here.
traps: Judging Ridge(alpha=1) against Lasso(alpha=1) as a fair fight. The objectives normalize the loss differently, so match effective shrinkage or validation error instead.
Fitting the scaler on all the data, or penalizing the intercept. Fit standardization on train only and keep the offset out of the penalty.
Reading lasso zeros as proof the dropped features carry no signal. Across resamples a correlated rival is selected instead, so report selection stability rather than one mask.

selfTest.q: Ridge(alpha=1) and Lasso(alpha=1) disagree sharply on standardized data. Is one implementation wrong?
selfTest.a: No. Ridge adds alpha ||w||^2 to the raw RSS, while Lasso adds alpha ||w||_1 to RSS/(2n), so the same number applies very different pressure. Sweep a path for each and compare by validation error.

selfTest.q: D2L 3.7 fits d = 200 features on 20 examples. Why does plain least squares break, and what does the L2 term change algebraically?
selfTest.a: With 200 features and 20 rows, X'X has rank at most 20, so infinitely many weight vectors fit training exactly. Adding alpha I makes X'X + alpha I invertible, so the solution is unique, and it trades some training fit for a smaller norm; as alpha goes to 0 it tends to the minimum-norm interpolant.

selfTest.q: Two features correlate at 0.999. Lasso keeps one with a large weight while ridge keeps both, shrunken. Why?
selfTest.a: When x1 and x2 are nearly equal, the loss depends almost only on w1 + w2. For a fixed sum with both weights positive, the L1 norm is the same for every split, so the lasso is nearly indifferent and small differences in the data tip it to a corner with one weight at zero. The L2 norm is smallest at an equal split, so ridge shares the weight.

selfTest.q: With 10 distinct x values, a degree-9 polynomial fits the training data exactly. Is it the best model?
selfTest.a: No. Zero training error does not imply low validation error: the exact fit can swing wildly between and beyond the points. That gap is what the underfitting-overfitting curve diagnoses.

units.title: Logistic regression and stable binary cross-entropy
outcomes: Derive the binary log likelihood, its prediction-error-times-input gradient, and the L2-penalized objective from a Gaussian prior.
Implement binary cross-entropy on logits that stays finite for extreme scores, with a gradient check.
Explain why there is no closed form, why concavity still guarantees a global optimum, and what C controls in sklearn.
units.why: Logistic regression turns a linear score into a probability claim, and its likelihood is the template for every neural classifier loss later. Getting the stable form right here prevents silent infinities everywhere after.

next.note: Generalize the sigmoid, the log likelihood and the stable loss to K classes.
Turn the fitted probabilities into cost-aware decisions.

study.title: Logistic regression: likelihood, gradient and regularization
study.locator: Sections 3.2 (conditional log likelihood with the gradient-ascent update from zero weights at eta 0.01) and 3.3 (L2-penalized log likelihood, Gaussian-prior MAP reading, penalized gradient rule 26)
study.depth: Read the likelihood and gradient derivations fully. Section 3.1 writes P(Y = 1|X) = 1/(1 + exp(w0 + sum wi Xi)), the opposite sign convention, and 3.2 flips Y in (24)-(25) to the usual form, so check signs when you compare. Skim 3.1; its Gaussian-to-sigmoid bridge returns in the LDA unit.

study.title: The logistic model and maximum likelihood
study.locator: Chapter 4, Sections 4.3.1 to 4.3.3 (pp. 139-141): the logistic model, likelihood (4.5) preferred over nonlinear least squares, and the Default-data arithmetic (balance $2,000 gives 58.6%)

study.title: Maximum likelihood and gradient-based fitting
study.locator: Section 22.7: The Maximum Likelihood Principle, then Numerical Optimization and the Negative Log-Likelihood with its set-up, initialize, descend and check-output worked example

study.title: Binary logistic loss, C semantics and solvers
study.locator: Section 1.1.11 with 1.1.11.1 (expit form, averaged binary cross-entropy plus r(w)/(S C); C = inf means no penalty) and 1.1.11.3 (solver-versus-penalty table; lbfgs is the default)

study.title: Estimating probabilities and decision boundaries
study.locator: Book Chapter 4: Estimating Probabilities through Decision Boundaries (printed pp. 168-174). Notebook 04 cells: Estimating Probabilities (iris virginica detector on petal width) and Decision Boundaries (boundary contour with C = 2)

focus: The gradient is prediction error times input, summed over rows. Mitchell ascends the summed log likelihood from zero weights; sklearn minimizes averaged cross-entropy plus an L2 term (C = 1.0 by default) with lbfgs. Their optima agree only when the penalties match, for example C = np.inf against Mitchell's unpenalized rule.
sklearn regularizes by default at C = 1.0 on an averaged loss, so its C is not a textbook lambda: smaller C means stronger penalty, and C = inf recovers the unpenalized fit.

Never exponentiate before logging. In float64 the sigmoid rounds to exactly 1.0 once z passes about 36.7, but to exactly 0 only below about -709.8, so the naive loss for y = 0 is already inf at z = 37, and at z = 36 it returns 36.044 instead of 36.0. The form max(z,0) - z y + log1p(exp(-|z|)) stays exact.
units.reproduce: Derive the (p - y) x gradient from the binary log likelihood. In float64 show the naive loss returns inf for (z = -800, y = 1) and already for (z = 40, y = 0), while max(z,0) - z y + log1p(exp(-|z|)) returns 800.0 and 40.0. Match your analytic gradient to central differences to 1e-8 on a 3-point demo.
traps: Equating sklearn C with a textbook lambda. C is inverse strength on an averaged loss, so doubling C halves the penalty; sample and class weights rescale the effective C through the total weight S.
Trusting probabilities from a near-unpenalized fit on nearly separable data. The likelihood keeps rewarding larger weights, so scores saturate toward exactly 0 and 1 without becoming more accurate.

Starting gradient ascent from large random weights for symmetry breaking. The objective is concave with one global optimum and Mitchell starts at zero; large starts only waste steps or overflow the first sigmoid.

selfTest.q: Why does logistic regression need iterative fitting when linear regression has a closed form?
selfTest.a: The sigmoid makes the log likelihood nonlinear in w with no analytic maximizer. The objective is concave, so gradient ascent still reaches the one global optimum.

selfTest.q: sklearn at default C = 1.0 disagrees with your zero-penalty NumPy fit. Which one is right?
selfTest.a: Both solve their stated objectives: sklearn minimizes averaged cross-entropy plus an L2 term at C = 1.0. Set C to inf or a very large value to recover the unpenalized fit.

selfTest.q: Training loss prints inf on the first epoch for a positive example with logit near -800. What happened, and what is the fix?
selfTest.a: The sigmoid underflowed to exactly 0 and log(0) is inf. A negative example fails much sooner: at logit 37 the sigmoid rounds to exactly 1 and log(1 - 1) is inf. Score in logits with max(z,0) - z y + log1p(exp(-|z|)) instead of exponentiating first.

selfTest.q: Recompute ISLP's 58.6% default risk for balance $2,000 from Table 4.1.
selfTest.a: z = -10.6513 + 0.0055 x 2000 = 0.3487; 1/(1 + exp(-0.3487)) = 0.586. A one-unit balance rise adds 0.0055 to the log odds.

units.title: Softmax regression and one-versus-rest
outcomes: Derive the softmax from K linear scores, its cross-entropy loss, and the prediction-error-times-input gradient.
Implement max-subtracted softmax and multiclass cross-entropy that stay finite on extreme logits.
Contrast joint multinomial fitting with one-versus-rest on parameter counts, calibration and solver limits.
units.why: Most real decisions choose among more than two outcomes. Softmax generalizes the sigmoid without breaking probability semantics, and one-versus-rest is the fallback every library reaches for when a solver only does binary.

next.note: Turn multiclass scores into decisions with costs attached.
Watch separation inflate the weights here exactly as in binary logistic regression.

study.title: Multinomial geometry, OvR solvers and calibration
study.locator: Section 1.1.11.2 (deliberate K-vector overparameterization, non-unique unpenalized solutions) and 1.1.11.3 with its solver table and Solvers' details (liblinear cannot fit a multinomial model, so multiclass use wraps it in OneVsRestClassifier; the multinomial loss is expected to calibrate better than one-versus-rest)

study.title: One-versus-rest in practice
study.locator: Book Chapter 3: Multiclass Classification (printed pp. 124-126). Notebook 03 cells: Multiclass Classification section: the SVC OvO-training note, OneVsRestClassifier with its 10 estimators, and the SGDClassifier multiclass run

focus: Softmax preserves order, so argmax needs no exponentials. Probabilities still need the max-subtracted form, because exp(1000) overflows to inf and inf divided by inf is nan.
sklearn fits K vectors for K classes on purpose, for symmetry under regularization. Without penalty that redundancy makes the solution non-unique, which is one more reason the default L2 matters.
One-versus-rest trains K binary problems and compares uncalibrated margins, while multinomial optimizes one joint loss. Expect worse-calibrated probabilities from the OvR scheme.
units.reproduce: Derive the (p_k - y_k) x gradient from the multiclass negative log likelihood. In NumPy show naive softmax of [1000, 1001, 999] returns [nan, nan, nan] while the max-subtracted form returns [0.2447, 0.6652, 0.0900]. Then do the D2L 4.4 exercise in float32, the dtype of D2L's PyTorch code: naive softmax of [-110, -111] returns [nan, nan] because both exponentials underflow to 0, and [-100, -101] gives 0.7297 instead of 0.7311 from subnormal rounding. In float64 both inputs still work; the cliff sits near -745.
traps: Copying the D2L 4.4 teaching softmax into real code. The page itself warns against verbatim use; framework implementations subtract the row maximum internally.
Calling OvR margins probabilities. One-versus-rest decision_function scores are not calibrated across the K classifiers; take predict_proba from a joint fit or calibrate afterwards.

Passing multi_class to LogisticRegression under sklearn 1.9. The parameter is gone and raises TypeError. Multiclass fits are multinomial under the default lbfgs, liblinear raises a ValueError on three or more classes, and one-versus-rest now means wrapping the estimator in OneVsRestClassifier.

selfTest.q: Why can argmax skip the softmax entirely?
selfTest.a: Softmax is monotone in each logit and preserves their order, so the largest logit is always the most probable class. Computing probabilities still needs the stable form.

selfTest.q: sklearn fits 3 vectors for 3 classes while Mitchell fits K - 1 = 2 linear functions. Is one of them wrong?
selfTest.a: No. K vectors deliberately overparameterize for symmetry under regularization, while K - 1 suffices because probabilities sum to one. Without penalty the K-vector solution is not unique.

selfTest.q: Naive softmax of [1000, 1001, 999] returns nan. Show the exact failure and the fix.
selfTest.a: Each exponential overflows to inf and inf/inf is nan. Subtract the row maximum first: exp([-1, 0, -2]) over its sum gives [0.2447, 0.6652, 0.0900] with the same argmax.

selfTest.q: liblinear is your only allowed solver on a 5-class problem. Which scheme, and what do you lose?
selfTest.a: One-versus-rest: wrap it in OneVsRestClassifier, which fits 5 binary estimators, because in sklearn 1.9 liblinear raises a ValueError on three or more classes. You lose the joint multinomial objective and should expect worse-calibrated probabilities.

units.title: Residual, leverage, separation and misspecification diagnostics
outcomes: Read residual-versus-fitted plots to separate nonlinearity, heteroscedasticity and outliers, and name the repair each prescribes.
Compute leverages from the hat matrix, flag high-leverage points, and distinguish leverage from influence.
Detect complete separation in logistic fits from runaway coefficients and saturated probabilities, and repair it with an explicit penalty.
units.why: A fit that converges is not a fit that is right. Diagnostics separate a broken model from a broken assumption, and separation is the one failure that looks like perfect success.

next.note: Set the decision rule only after the fit survives diagnostics.
Fold residual and slice analysis into the evaluation harness.

study.title: Error-only confusion views
study.locator: Book Chapter 3: Error Analysis (printed pp. 126-130). Notebook 03 cells: Error Analysis section: row-normalized matrices, then error-only views with sample_weight, normalized by row and by column

focus: Leverage measures position in x-space, not wrongness. The x = 10 point in a 0-to-2 design carries leverage 0.98 out of p = 2 while anchoring the slope; residuals measure wrongness, and influence needs both.

Patterns have signatures. Curvature in residual-versus-fitted means nonlinearity, a funnel means heteroscedasticity, and isolated large standardized residuals mean outliers; each prescribes a different repair.

Separation shows as coefficients that keep growing as C is relaxed, with probabilities glued to 0 and 1. On x = 0,1,2,3 with y = 0,0,1,1 the slope is 0.96 at C = 1 and 9.31 at C = 1e3. At C = 1e6 lbfgs stops at 16.57 under its default tol = 1e-4 with no warning, while tol = 1e-12 reaches 21.50. The fix is a finite penalty, not more iterations.
units.reproduce: From a blank file compute hat diagonals on the design [[1,0],[1,1],[1,2],[1,10]] and match leverages [0.4183, 0.3307, 0.2749, 0.9761] summing to p = 2. Then fit LogisticRegression on x = [0,1,2,3] with y = [0,0,1,1] at C = 1, 1e3 and 1e6 with scikit-learn 1.9.1 defaults and match slopes [0.9583], [9.3057] and [16.5719]. Refit C = 1e6 with tol=1e-12 and watch the slope move to 21.4953: under separation the stopping rule, not the data, sets the weights.
traps: Deleting every high-leverage point. Leverage is not guilt: a far-x point with a small residual anchors the fit. Act on influence, which combines residual and leverage (Cook's distance), not on position alone.

Reading saturated 0 and 1 probabilities as a great classifier. Under separation the likelihood rewards ever-larger weights, so perfect scores signal an unidentified model rather than a solved problem.

Raising max_iter or C to force a separated fit to converge. The penalized optimum keeps moving outward as C grows, and under the default tol lbfgs stops early without a ConvergenceWarning, so a quiet fit proves nothing. Keep the penalty finite or collect overlapping cases.

selfTest.q: Residual-versus-fitted shows a U shape. What is wrong, and what changes?
selfTest.a: Nonlinearity the linear form cannot express. Add polynomial or interaction terms rather than collecting more data for the same line.

selfTest.q: The x = 10 point has leverage 0.98 out of p = 2. Should it be deleted?
selfTest.a: Not on leverage alone. It dominates the slope estimate but a small residual there is informative. Check influence by refitting without it before deciding.

selfTest.q: Logistic coefficients keep growing as C is relaxed (0.96, 9.31, 16.57 at C = 1, 1e3, 1e6) and the probabilities print as 0 or 1. Diagnose and repair.
selfTest.a: Complete separation: the maximum likelihood weights are unbounded and only the penalty keeps them finite, so the penalized optimum moves outward roughly in proportion to log C. Keep C finite, confirm the weights hold under a tighter tol, and look for overlapping cases to collect.

selfTest.q: Standardized residuals fan out as fitted values grow. Name the violation and one valid response.
selfTest.a: Heteroscedasticity, non-constant error variance. Transform the response, model the variance, or use variance-robust inference; adding polynomial terms does not fix it.

units.title: LDA, QDA and generative versus discriminative classifiers
outcomes: Derive the LDA discriminant from Gaussian class conditionals with shared covariance and show the boundary is linear.
Derive the QDA and Gaussian naive Bayes discriminants, and state the exact assumption that turns one into the other.
Contrast generative and discriminative fitting on parameter counts, small-sample behavior and robustness to violated assumptions.
units.why: LDA, QDA, naive Bayes and logistic regression all draw linear-or-quadratic boundaries from different assumptions. Seeing which assumption buys which boundary tells you what breaks first when the data disobeys.

next.note: Shrink the Gaussian assumption to diagonal covariance and smoothed counts.
Weight discriminant scores by class priors before deciding.

study.title: Generative versus discriminative classifiers
study.locator: Sections 1 (Bayes-rule learning and the 2(2n - 1) parameter count), 2.1-2.2 (conditional independence and the naive Bayes derivation), 3.1 (Gaussian naive Bayes implies the logistic form) and 4 (discriminative versus generative, asymptotic identity, Ng and Jordan rates)

study.title: LDA and QDA formulation and solvers
study.locator: Section 1.2.2 (Bayes rule, Gaussian class conditionals, QDA log-posterior, LDA linear form with coef_ and intercept_, and the QDA-with-diagonal-covariance equals GaussianNB note) and 1.2.5 (svd is the default solver)

study.title: LDA and QDA lab on the Smarket data
study.locator: Linear Discriminant Analysis and Quadratic Discriminant Analysis sections: fits, posterior values and confusion matrices beside the logistic fit

focus: LDA log odds are linear in x because the shared covariance cancels every quadratic term; QDA keeps one covariance per class, so its boundary is quadratic with cross terms.

Gaussian naive Bayes is QDA with diagonal class covariances. If each feature's variance is also shared across classes, it becomes LDA with a diagonal shared covariance (ISLP 4.5.1). Naive Bayes in general, with any per-feature densities, and QDA do not nest: naive Bayes log odds are additive in the features, while QDA's contain products of feature pairs.

Logistic regression and LDA posit the same linear log-odds form but fit it differently: LDA estimates class Gaussians and priors while logistic maximizes the conditional likelihood. Expect LDA to win when normality holds and logistic when it does not.
units.reproduce: Write the LDA discriminant delta_k(x) = x' Sigma^{-1} mu_k - mu_k' Sigma^{-1} mu_k / 2 + log pi_k from the Gaussian log posterior. Build the two-Gaussian demo with default_rng(3): 40 standard normal points around [0,0], then 40 around [2,2]. Match sklearn LDA priors [0.5, 0.5], training score 0.95, coefficients [1.927, 2.229] and intercept -4.070.
traps: Fitting QDA with too few rows per class. Each class covariance comes from that class's rows alone, and with p or fewer rows per class (the class mean uses one) it is singular. Use QDA's reg_param or shrinkage with the eigen solver, or LDA with shrinkage.
Calling LDA parameter-free. It exposes no tuning knob by default but still estimates K means, a shared covariance and priors, which overfit small samples.

Assuming discriminative always wins with enough data. Logistic regression often has the lower asymptotic error under misspecification, but per Ng and Jordan naive Bayes approaches its own asymptote in order log n examples versus order n for logistic regression, where n is the number of features. So LDA and naive Bayes often win when training data are scarce.

selfTest.q: Write the two-class LDA decision rule and name each estimated quantity.
selfTest.a: Assign argmax over k of x' Sigma^{-1} mu_k - mu_k' Sigma^{-1} mu_k/2 + log pi_k: class means, one shared covariance and priors. The x-quadratic terms cancel because Sigma is shared, leaving a linear boundary.

selfTest.q: When does QDA collapse to Gaussian naive Bayes, and when does Gaussian naive Bayes collapse toward LDA?
selfTest.a: QDA restricted to diagonal class covariances is Gaussian naive Bayes. Gaussian naive Bayes whose per-feature variances are shared across classes is LDA with a diagonal shared covariance. General naive Bayes and QDA do not nest: one is additive, the other has pairwise products.

selfTest.q: 50 training points, 20 features, roughly Gaussian classes. LDA, QDA or logistic first?
selfTest.a: LDA, possibly with shrinkage. QDA must estimate two 20-by-20 covariances from about 25 points each, and logistic fits 21 weights discriminatively with higher variance. Revisit logistic if normality is badly violated and more data arrives.

selfTest.q: State the Ng and Jordan sample-complexity contrast and its practical consequence.
selfTest.a: Naive Bayes approaches its asymptotic error in order log n training examples and logistic regression needs order n, where n is the number of features, not samples. So naive Bayes often wins on small training sets, while logistic regression, with its usually lower asymptotic error, wins once data are plentiful.

units.title: Naive Bayes: event models, smoothing and log-space scoring
outcomes: Derive the naive Bayes decision rule from conditional independence and count its free parameters per event model.
Implement Bernoulli naive Bayes with Laplace smoothing and log-space scoring, handling unseen values and single-class training data.
Select the event model (Bernoulli, multinomial, Gaussian) from the feature type and state what each independence assumption ignores.
units.why: Naive Bayes is the smallest complete probabilistic classifier: counting, smoothing and log-space scoring in one place. Its failure mode, confident scores from false independence, previews every calibration problem later.

next.note: Correct the overconfident scores before thresholding them.
Score the outputs with log loss and Brier rather than accuracy.

study.title: Gaussian naive Bayes lab on Smarket
study.locator: Naive Bayes section: GaussianNB fit on Smarket with classes_ and class_prior_ readouts

focus: Smoothing is a MAP estimate under a Dirichlet prior, not a hack. Mitchell's (count + l)/(total + lJ) at l = 1 is Laplace, and BernoulliNB's alpha = 1.0 is the same add-one per value; without it one unseen value zeroes the whole product.

Bernoulli penalizes absent indicator features while multinomial ignores absent counts. That is why occurrence vectors can beat count vectors on short documents, and why the two models are not interchangeable.
Score in log space always. A product of 1100 halves is exactly 0.0 in float64 while the log sum stays finite at -762.46; argmax needs only the sums.
units.reproduce: Derive the MAP rule argmax_y P(y) prod_i P(x_i|y) from conditional independence. From a blank file implement Bernoulli naive Bayes with alpha = 1.0: on X = [[1,0],[1,1],[0,0],[0,1]] with y = [1,1,0,0] match sklearn feature_log_prob_ rows [-1.3863, -0.6931] for class 0 and [-0.2877, -0.6931] for class 1, predict [1] for [[1,0]], and return the majority class when trained on one class only.
traps: Feeding counts to BernoulliNB or magnitudes to a binary model without thought. BernoulliNB binarizes continuous input at binarize = 0.0 by default, silently turning magnitudes into presence flags.
Multiplying raw probabilities and comparing. Beyond underflow, one unsmoothed zero vetoes the class; sum logs and smooth first.
Reading predict_proba as calibrated confidence. The guide calls naive Bayes a bad estimator: use the scores to rank, then threshold or calibrate downstream.

selfTest.q: A test word never appeared in training. What happens with and without smoothing?
selfTest.a: Without smoothing its likelihood is 0 and the whole class product is 0 regardless of other evidence. With Laplace alpha = 1 it contributes a small nonzero factor that rarely decides the argmax alone.

selfTest.q: When does Bernoulli beat multinomial on text, and why?
selfTest.a: With occurrence vectors on short documents: Bernoulli explicitly penalizes the non-occurrence of indicator words while multinomial ignores absent counts. sklearn advises evaluating both when time permits.

selfTest.q: Write the smoothed discrete likelihood and name its prior.
selfTest.a: (count + l)/(class total + lJ): the MAP estimate under a symmetric Dirichlet prior with parameters l + 1, equivalently the posterior mean under parameters l; l = 1 is Laplace. Priors smooth the same way with lK in the denominator.

selfTest.q: XOR data with labels [0,1,1,0]. Does naive Bayes succeed, and which assumption fails?
selfTest.a: No. Each feature alone is uninformative about the label, so conditional independence destroys the interaction. Allowing explicit dependence between the inputs fixes it.

units.title: Probability estimates, class priors and asymmetric thresholds
outcomes: Derive the cost-optimal threshold from class probabilities and misclassification costs, and show why 0.5 is only optimal for symmetric costs.
Adjust decisions for changed class priors without refitting, through the prior-odds correction.
Measure precision-recall and ROC tradeoffs on fixed validation data and select a threshold from stated costs.
units.why: A probability is not a decision. The same fitted scores need different thresholds under different costs and different priors, and 0.5 is a cost claim most projects never stated.

next.note: Extend cost-sensitive thresholds to imbalance and prevalence change.
Recalibrate the estimates this unit learns to distrust.

Notebook 03 cells: Precision/Recall Trade-off section (precision_recall_curve on the MNIST 5-detector, the threshold-3000 demo, idx_for_90_precision) and The ROC Curve section with the 90%-precision operating point

study.locator: Section 1.1.11 introduction (predicted probability becomes a classifier at a threshold, by default 0.5), Binary Case (sample and class weights rescale the effective C through S) and Solvers details (joint multinomial loss calibrates better than OvR)

study.title: Priors inside the discriminant scores
study.locator: Section 1.2.2 (posteriors combine class conditionals with P(y = k); LDA adds log P(y = k) to the discriminant) and 1.2.4 (shrinkage as the small-sample stabilizer for those estimates)

focus: sklearn predicts the positive class at 0.5 by default. That bakes in equal costs and matched priors; any asymmetric cost matrix moves the optimal threshold to C_FP/(C_FP + C_FN).
Naive Bayes scores rank well but estimate badly, and OvR margins are not calibrated across classifiers. Thresholding an uncalibrated score encodes its bias as policy.
Priors shift without refitting: multiply the posterior odds by the new-over-old prior-odds ratio. Thresholds move with prevalence even when the feature evidence stays fixed.
units.reproduce: Derive t = C_FP/(C_FP + C_FN) from predicting 1 exactly when p times C_FN exceeds (1 - p) times C_FP, and show costs of 1 and 9 give t = 0.1. From a blank script recompute precisions, recalls and thresholds with precision_recall_curve on binary scores and implement the first-index rule that finds the 90%-precision threshold.
traps: Tuning the threshold on the test set. Thresholds are fitted parameters: select on validation, report once on test, or the reported precision is optimistic.

Comparing thresholds across models with different score scales. A 0.3 cutoff on calibrated probabilities means something different from 3000 on raw margins; compare at matched precision or recall, not matched knob values.
Keeping 0.5 after reweighting classes. Class and sample weights change the score scale and the effective penalty, so retune the threshold after any weighting change.

selfTest.q: False negatives cost 9 times false positives. Which threshold, and why not 0.5?
selfTest.a: t = 1/(1 + 9) = 0.1: predict positive whenever p exceeds 0.1. The 0.5 default assumes equal costs and would miss cheap-to-catch positives.

selfTest.q: Deployment prevalence of positives halves with the same feature evidence. How do the optimal decisions change without refitting?
selfTest.a: Posterior odds are the likelihood ratio times the prior odds, so every case's posterior odds are multiplied by the new-over-old prior-odds ratio, about one half when positives are rare. Fewer cases clear any fixed threshold; recompute posteriors with the new priors, or move the threshold equivalently, instead of reusing the old cutoff.

selfTest.q: Two detectors both report 90% precision, one at margin 3000 and one at probability 0.42. Which threshold is better?
selfTest.a: The knobs are incomparable across scales. Compare recall at matched precision, or expected cost, on the same validation data.

selfTest.q: The guide warns naive Bayes is a bad estimator. What breaks if its raw scores are thresholded at 0.5?
selfTest.a: Ranking can be good while false independence pushes absolute scores to extremes, so 0.5 lands in the wrong place. Set the threshold from measured precision and recall, or calibrate first.
